contentBlocks.body: In JavaScript each project has its own node_modules folder, so two projects can use different versions of the same library. Python installs packages into one site-packages directory per interpreter, so by default every project on the machine shares them. A virtual environment (venv) fixes that: it is a folder containing its own python executable and its own site-packages.

contentBlocks.code:
$ python -m venv .venv            # create the environment in ./.venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate       # macOS/Linux
> .venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows
(.venv) $ python -m pip install requests
(.venv) $ python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
(.venv) $ deactivate

contentBlocks.body: Activating only changes your shell's PATH so that python and pip point at the venv's copies. You can skip activation and call .venv/bin/python directly; that is what editors and CI scripts often do. Running pip as python -m pip guarantees you install into the interpreter you think you are using.

pip is the package installer, like npm install. PyPI is the package index, like the npm registry. A requirements.txt lists pinned versions for reproducible installs (roughly a lockfile). Modern projects declare their metadata and dependencies in pyproject.toml, which plays the role of package.json; tools such as uv, Poetry, or pip-tools add real lockfiles on top.

contentBlocks.code:
# requirements.txt
requests==2.32.3
pytest==8.3.2

$ python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

contentBlocks.body: Never commit the .venv folder; add it to .gitignore, just like node_modules. Commit requirements.txt or pyproject.toml plus a lockfile, and recreate the environment from them.

Installing packages globally with sudo pip install can break tools your operating system depends on. Many Linux distributions now refuse it with an 'externally managed environment' error. Use a venv instead.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What problem does a Python virtual environment solve?

choices: it makes Python code run faster
it compiles Python to machine code
it replaces the need for pip
it gives each project its own interpreter and installed packages
payload.answer: it gives each project its own interpreter and installed packages
payload.explanation: Without a venv, every project shares one site-packages directory, so version conflicts are likely.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What does activating a venv actually change?

choices: your shell's PATH, so python and pip resolve to the venv's copies
the contents of your source files
the version of PyPI you download from
payload.answer: your shell's PATH, so python and pip resolve to the venv's copies
payload.explanation: Activation is a convenience. Calling .venv/bin/python directly has the same effect without activating.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Which file is closest to package.json in a modern Python project?

payload.explanation: pyproject.toml holds project metadata, dependencies, and tool configuration.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why prefer python -m pip install over a bare pip install?

choices: it installs into exactly the interpreter that python points to
payload.answer: it installs into exactly the interpreter that python points to
payload.explanation: A bare pip on PATH may belong to a different Python than the one that will run your code.

payload.text: The command python -m ____ .venv creates a virtual environment in the .venv folder.
